topic: Agent Development Kit and Agent Engine
question: An airline wants to build a travel-assistance agent that can check flight status, rebook passengers and issue vouchers by calling internal APIs, with a planner agent delegating to specialized sub-agents. Option D achieves the goal but requires operating a cluster and building session and observability plumbing that Agent Engine already provides.
hint: Core Rule (Agent Development Kit and Agent Engine): The Agent Development Kit is Google's open-source, code-first Python framework for building tool-using and multi-agent systems, with local testing, and Vertex AI Agent Engine (part of Vertex AI Agent Builder) is the managed runtime that hosts ADK agents with session management, scaling and tracing, so developers get exactly the workflow described without servers.

question: An e-commerce company's customer-support application sends every user question to Gemini on Vertex AI together with the same 60,000-token product-policy document as context. Monthly token costs have tripled, and most questions are simple. The company wants to cut cost significantly without degrading answer quality on complex questions. Which two actions should you take? Route simple questions to a smaller, cheaper Gemini Flash-class model and reserve the larger model for complex questions, using a lightweight classifier or the model's own routing.
Raise the temperature parameter to reduce the number of output tokens generated.
Deploy Gemini to a dedicated GPU endpoint so that you pay per hour instead of per token.
Switch from Gemini to Imagen because image models have a lower per-request price.

Option C is wrong because temperature controls randomness, not response length. Option D is not possible; Gemini is served as a managed API and is not deployable to customer GPU endpoints. Option E is nonsensical because Imagen generates images and cannot answer support questions.
hint: Core Rule (Gemini cost optimization): Context caching stores a large, frequently reused prefix (such as the policy document) so subsequent requests pay a discounted rate for those cached tokens, and model routing sends easy queries to a cheaper Flash-class model while keeping quality for hard ones, which together address the dominant cost drivers (cost optimization pillar).
